title: Why We Have Government
short: Governments keep order, provide security and public goods, protect rights and settle disputes; the Preamble lists six purposes, from "a more perfect Union" to "the Blessings of Liberty."
trouble: Students confuse the purposes of government with its powers. A purpose is a goal ("insure domestic Tranquility"); a power is a means (to tax, to raise an army).

blocks.html: Every group of people that lives together has to settle the same questions. Who keeps the peace? Who defends against attack? Who builds the roads no one family could build? Who decides a quarrel when two neighbors both say they are right? Government is the set of people and institutions with the authority to make rules for a society and to enforce them. In colonial self-government you saw Americans running their own assemblies; this course asks what all that machinery is for.

People accept rules and taxes because government can do things that are hard or impossible to do alone. It keeps order, so disputes are settled by law instead of by force. It provides security against threats from inside and outside. It supplies public goods, such as national defense, clean water systems and roads, which everyone benefits from and no one can easily be kept from using, so private sellers tend to provide too little of them. And in the American tradition it exists to protect rights. Thinkers disagree about which purpose matters most; the next topics give their arguments.

marks.note: Unite the states more closely than the Articles of Confederation had.
Fair laws and courts to settle disputes.
The well-being of the people as a whole.
Protect freedom, for "ourselves and our Posterity" (future generations).

blocks.cap: The Preamble names six purposes. Tap each one.

blocks.html: The Preamble lists six purposes (goals) of the government: a more perfect Union, Justice, domestic Tranquility, the common defence, the general Welfare and the Blessings of Liberty. The articles that follow grant the powers (the means) to reach them.

head: Purpose in the Preamble
In plain words
A power that serves it
rows: regulate commerce among the states (Article I)
create federal courts (Articles I and III)
call out the militia to put down an insurrection (Article I)
raise armies and maintain a navy (Article I)
limits such as the Bill of Rights restrain the government itself
blocks.cap: Purposes are ends; powers are means.

blocks.title: Purpose or power?
blocks.q: Article I, Section 8 says Congress may "lay and collect Taxes." Is that a purpose or a power?
steps: Ask what the phrase names: an outcome the government aims at, or an action it is allowed to take.
Collecting taxes is an action, a tool. It names no goal by itself.
Taxes pay for the common defence and the general Welfare, which are purposes.
blocks.a: A power. It serves purposes such as the common defence and the general Welfare.

blocks.title: Matching an action to a purpose
blocks.q: A federal court decides a contract dispute between a company in Ohio and a company in Texas. Which purpose in the Preamble does that serve?
steps: The court settles a quarrel by law, so neither side has to use force or rely on a court that might favor its own state.
Fair settlement of disputes is the meaning of "establish Justice."

blocks.html: Mixing up purposes and powers. "Provide for the common defence" is a goal; "raise and support Armies" is a power that serves it. Quick check: a purpose answers "why?"; a power answers "what may the government do?"
